title: Should Welders Care About History Class — or Algebra 2? Or Literature?
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart takes up a common motivational obstacle: students and parents who say a course is worthless because it does not connect to a future job. He treats these remarks as expressions of a missing value belief, not attacks, and tells teachers to begin with empathy, recalling his own resistant reaction to a pre-packaged PD. From there he asks teachers to become apologists for education, borrowing the model of C. S. Lewis, and to build twenty or more honest arguments for why their class matters apart from employment. His claim is that public education was never meant simply to prepare people for jobs and that teachers keep it from losing its soul one interaction at a time. He also points to Hulleman's build-connections intervention and teacher credibility as complements.
points: When students dismiss a course as irrelevant, treat it as a statement about value, not as a personal attack.
Respond first with empathy, remembering how it feels to be forced into work that seems pointless.
Teachers must become apologists for education, arguing to heart and imagination as well as to logic.
Prepare twenty or more arguments for why the work matters beyond job relevance.
A system that only prepares workers has lost its soul, so teachers should speak a bigger vision of education.
quotes: First, we empathize. It is painful to feel that you’re being forced to do something that has no relevance or value to your life. Think about the last PD or meeting you went to that felt like this.

Any time our students say, “This is dumb,” “This is pointless,” “This is annoying,” our work as a professional begins. The professional doesn’t say, “Well fine then, this child is just unmotivated and apathetic and there’s nothing I can do.
We’ve got to become apologists for education. An apologist is a defender, an upholder, a proponent of something controversial.

In 2019, it actually is a minority worldview that an education is an inherently beautiful and unending and emancipatory thing. To say, “Well, an education’s value isn’t just what’s measured on the test, isn’t just what’s going to be useful in your job,” is to invite scoffing.
So own the reasons you became a teacher to begin with. Grapple earnestly with the gaps between what an education ought to be and what the system currently makes it out to be.

From the empathetic position — and all the great apologists work from there — engage with the concerns of your would-be welder in the British Literature class, your hopes-to-work-in-HVAC student in Chemistry. And as I often recommend when I’m speaking with teachers, come up with not only one, not only five, but twenty or more arguments for why the work you do in your class is worthy work despite its lack of direct connection to someone’s future job.

The key point with our welder friend is that the public education experiment was never meant to simply prepare people for jobs. A system just focused on that one outcome is a system that has lost its soul.
